props.title: Valkyrie
props.initialSlug: Dare the unthinkable. Defy the Reich.

sections.content: Valkyrie stands as one of Hollywood's most gripping depictions of the German resistance during WWII. Tom Cruise delivers a taut performance as Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg, the aristocratic officer who spearheaded Operation Valkyrie - the failed July 20, 1944 assassination attempt against Hitler. Director Bryan Singer brings the same tension-building expertise he showed in The Usual Suspects (1995), crafting a historical thriller that maintains suspense even when we know the outcome. The film's attention to period detail, from the Wehrmacht uniforms to the Wolf's Lair setting, creates an immersive backdrop for this tale of moral courage.

sections.content: The film fits into a vital subgenre of WWII resistance films that emerged in the post-war era. While The Great Escape (1963) and Where Eagles Dare (1968) took more action-oriented approaches, Valkyrie follows the sobering path of films like Army of Shadows (1969) and Black Book (2006) in examining the moral complexities and personal costs of resistance. Singer's decision to have the actors speak in their natural accents rather than affected German ones helps emphasize the universal human elements of the story.

What sets Valkyrie apart is its focus on the technical and bureaucratic aspects of the conspiracy. Like The Day of the Jackal (1973), it meticulously details the planning and near-execution of an assassination attempt. The film's strengths lie in showing how Stauffenberg and his co-conspirators attempted to use the Nazi regime's own emergency protocols against it, turning Operation Valkyrie from a contingency plan into a tool for coup d'état. sections.content: The film raises compelling questions about duty, loyalty and moral action under tyranny. Like A Hidden Life (2019), it explores what drives individuals to risk everything in opposition to evil. The supporting cast, including Kenneth Branagh, Bill Nighy and Tom Wilkinson, brings depth to the various Wehrmacht officers wrestling with their consciences. Their internal struggles echo similar themes in The Pianist (2002) and Schindler's List (1993) about personal responsibility in the face of systemic evil.
